newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian protesters take back the streets.
newsitem.headline: Serbian protesters take back the streets.

text.p: Triumphant Serbian demonstrators said they had won back the streets of the capital Belgrade after riot police apparently gave up pushing them onto pavements to enforce a ban on marches.

Tens of thousands of pro-democracy protesters from outlying districts converged on the city centre on Tuesday evening, blowing whistles and dancing to the beat of drums as they made their way to Republic Square.
Some 50,000 to 60,000 people cheered leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, who told them 10 weeks of protests were wearing out the police, not the demonstrators.
"There is no police cordon which can hold back a Serbia which knows what it wants -- our future, democracy, a renaissance of Serbia," said Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic.
Riot police formed cordons this month to force protests onto pavements. But they relented on Tuesday evening, allowing marchers to block traffic and cross a main bridge spanning the Sava river.

More than 70 days of protests demanding the ruling Socialists recognise the results of November municipal elections have won Western support and grown into a referendum on the authoritarian rule of Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic.
"This regime is already dead, and Serbia will never be the same again -- we don't know the exact date it will fall, but it will be soon," Vesna Pesic, another Zajendo leader, told the crowd.
A Russian envoy held talks with Zajedno representatives and Milosevic in an attempt to broker a compromise but there was no report of a breakthrough.

First Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov met Milosevic on Tuesday and Belgrade government media said the two agreed that a state's internal problems should not be resolved by "external interference".
The United States has spearheaded Western pressure on the Socialists to concede defeat in the local polls.
Experts sent by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) also concluded the opposition had won in 14 of the country's biggest towns, including Belgrade.

Milosevic has remained aloof and out of the public eye despite the deepening crisis. His state television, despised by opposition supporters, portrays the Zajedno coalition as traitors plotting with foreign powers and ethnic Albanians to "destabilise" Serbia.
The protests have exposed divisions within Milosevic's ranks and criticism from the republic of Montenegro, Serbia's junior partner in the Yugoslav federation.

Socialist officials, trying to defuse the political crisis, have promised a "reshuffle" of government posts. They announced on Tuesday the sacking of the directors of the state power company and telephone company.
Milosevic's delaying tactics, media attacks and sporadic police beatings have so far failed to stifle the protests.
The former communist party chief has lost support in industrial towns which were once socialist strongholds.
The Yugoslav army has told student leaders it will not shoot at demonstrators and the formerly pro-government Serbian Orthodox church has sided with the opposition.
Even members of his ruling apparatus have begun hedging their bets, sensing the president is no longer assured of an indefinite reign.

A former U.S. ambassador to old Yugoslavia, Warren Zimmerman, told CNN on Tuesday that Milosevic's days were numbered. "The opposition has the upper hand. Milosevic is losing day by day, to the point where I think in a few months we may be looking at him as history," he said.
